lessons.title: Buying & Selling Basics
lessons.description: Learn the fundamentals of entering and exiting trades — from DCA to stop-losses.

content.text: How to Enter and Exit a Trade

Trading sounds simple — buy low, sell high. In practice, it requires discipline, a clear plan, and the right tools. Before you trade, you should know how to buy effectively, protect yourself with stop-losses, and take profit at the right time.
💰 Buying Strategies

**Market buy** — Buys immediately at the current best price. Fast but you have no price control.

**Limit buy** — You set a target price below the market. The order waits until price drops to your level. Better price, but no guarantee it fills.

**Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA)** — Invest a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals regardless of price. Reduces the impact of volatility over time. Great for beginners.

**Buying the dip** — Purchasing after a price decline, expecting recovery. Risky if the decline continues.
📤 Selling & Holding Strategies

**HODL** — Hold through volatility, betting on long-term appreciation. Famously derived from a typo of 'hold.'

**Take-profit order** — Automatically sells when price hits your target. Removes emotion from the exit.

**Stop-loss order** — Automatically sells if price drops to a set level. Limits your downside.

**Trading styles by timeframe:**
- Day trading: opens and closes same day
- Swing trading: holds days to weeks
- Position trading: holds months to years

lessons.title: Technical Analysis Introduction
lessons.description: Learn chart patterns, indicators, and how traders use price history to make decisions.

content.text: Reading the Market Through Charts

**Technical analysis (TA)** is the practice of analyzing price history, volume, and chart patterns to predict future price movements. TA traders believe that all known information is already reflected in the price, and that history tends to repeat itself.
📐 Trend Lines & Patterns

**Trend line** — A line connecting price highs (downtrend) or lows (uptrend) to show direction.
**Breakout** — When price moves decisively above resistance or below support, often with high volume.
**Head and Shoulders** — A reversal pattern: three peaks where the middle is highest. Signals a trend change from bullish to bearish.
**Double Top** — Two peaks at similar price levels. Signals a bearish reversal.
**Double Bottom** — Two troughs at similar levels. Signals a bullish reversal.
📊 Key Indicators

**MACD** (Moving Average Convergence Divergence) — Measures momentum by comparing two moving averages. A bullish crossover signals potential upward momentum.
**Bollinger Bands** — Three lines (middle MA, upper, lower) that expand with volatility. Price near the upper band = overbought; near lower band = oversold.
**Death Cross** — When the 50-day MA crosses below the 200-day MA. A bearish long-term signal.
**Golden Cross** — When the 50-day MA crosses above the 200-day MA. A bullish long-term signal.

lessons.title: Fundamental Analysis in Crypto
lessons.description: Learn to evaluate crypto projects beyond price — teams, tokenomics, and on-chain data.

content.text: Is This Project Worth Anything?

**Fundamental analysis (FA)** evaluates whether a cryptocurrency has real long-term value by examining the project itself — not just its price. In crypto, this means analyzing the team, technology, tokenomics, community, and real-world usage.
🔍 What to Evaluate

**Whitepaper** — The technical document explaining the project's purpose, technology, and token distribution. A vague or copied whitepaper is a red flag.

**Team** — Are the founders public, credible, and experienced? Anonymous teams carry higher risk.

**Tokenomics** — How many tokens exist? Who holds them? Are large portions locked or vested? High team allocations and no vesting = risk.

**Community & Adoption** — Is the project actually being used? GitHub activity, transaction counts, and TVL (Total Value Locked) show real traction.
⚠️ Red Flags

**Rug pull** — Developers launch a project, raise funds, then disappear with investor money. Common with anonymous teams and no liquidity lock.

**No real utility** — Does the token actually do anything? Many tokens exist purely for speculation.

**NVT Ratio** — Network Value to Transactions ratio. A very high NVT suggests the coin's value is disconnected from actual usage.

**Roadmap** — Does the project have clear, achievable milestones? Vague roadmaps without timelines are a concern.

lessons.title: Market Cycles & Sentiment
lessons.description: Understand the four phases of market cycles and how to read investor sentiment.

content.text: Markets Move in Predictable Phases

Cryptocurrency markets, like all asset markets, move through recognizable cycles. Understanding which phase you're in helps you make smarter decisions — buying when others are fearful, and being cautious when others are greedy.
🔄 The Four Phases of a Market Cycle

1. **Accumulation** — Smart money quietly buys at low prices while the public is still pessimistic after the last bear market. Low volatility, little media attention.
2. **Markup** — Prices rise as more investors notice. FOMO kicks in. Altcoin season often happens here.
3. **Distribution** — Early investors sell to late buyers near the peak. Prices become volatile. Mainstream media covers crypto enthusiastically.
4. **Decline** — Prices fall. Late buyers panic sell. The cycle resets.
😱😀 Measuring Sentiment

**Fear & Greed Index** — Measures crypto market sentiment from 0 (extreme fear) to 100 (extreme greed). Extreme fear can signal a buying opportunity; extreme greed often precedes corrections.

**Bitcoin Halving** — Every ~4 years, Bitcoin's block reward is halved. This reduces new supply and has historically preceded bull markets.

**Stock-to-Flow (S2F)** — A model predicting Bitcoin's price based on its scarcity. As supply growth slows, the model suggests prices rise.

In crypto, **when Bitcoin falls sharply, altcoins usually fall faster.** When Bitcoin rises, altcoins often follow — but with more volatility.

lessons.title: Trading Psychology
lessons.description: Master the mental side of trading — emotions, biases, and building consistent habits.

content.text: The Hardest Part of Trading Is Your Own Mind

Most traders who fail don't fail because they lack knowledge — they fail because of their emotions. Greed, fear, and ego cause traders to break their own rules at the worst possible moment. Trading psychology is about building systems to take emotions out of the equation.
🧠 Common Psychological Pitfalls

**Overtrading** — Trading too often out of boredom or to 'make back' losses. Each trade has fees and risk.

**Revenge trading** — Immediately taking another trade after a loss, emotionally trying to recover. This compounds losses.

**Confirmation bias** — Only seeking information that supports what you already believe about a trade.

**Loss aversion** — Holding losing trades too long hoping to 'break even,' while cutting winners too early.

**FOMO** — Chasing a price after it's already moved significantly, entering at the worst time.
📓 Building Good Habits

**Trading journal** — Record every trade: why you entered, your stop-loss, target, and the outcome. Reviewing your journal reveals patterns in your mistakes.

**Paper trading** — Practice with simulated money before risking real capital. Many exchanges offer this.

**Risk-reward ratio** — Only take trades where potential gain is at least twice the potential loss (1:2 minimum). This means you can be wrong 40% of the time and still profit.

**Golden rule** — Only trade with money you can afford to lose completely. Never trade rent money.
